label: business valuation and sale
overview: Business valuation scenarios require the advisor to place the seller in the negotiation seat of the purchaser — viewing the business through a buyer's lens before setting any asking price. The underlying method is asset-based valuation (tangible and intangible assets), but simply adding assets and applying a profit multiplier is insufficient and can lead to overvaluation. Every valuation must be tested against three reality checks — Serviceability, Goodwill Repayment Period, and Performance Variance — to ensure the price is bankable for the purchaser. Deal structures such as MBO (Management Buy Out), BIMBO (Buy In Management Buy Out), and Newco (a new company vehicle created to acquire the business) all require the same valuation discipline before deal terms can be structured.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Is the client seeking to sell their business, purchase a business, or understand what their business is currently worth — and what is the intended buyer profile?
diagnostic_entry.seller_seeking_valuation: Start with Steps 1–3 of the methodology to establish Adjusted Net Profit and Super Profit. Then apply the 3-Point Sensitivities to test whether the indicative value range is bankable. The seller must be prepared to evidence every component of the asking price.
diagnostic_entry.buyer_assessing_a_purchase: Apply the same 6-step framework from the purchaser's perspective. Focus first on Serviceability — can the business cash surplus service the debt required to buy it? Then assess the Goodwill Payback Period and the transferability of intangible assets.
diagnostic_entry.deal_structure_question: If the deal involves an MBO, BIMBO, or Newco structure, the valuation framework applies identically — the structure determines how the purchase is funded and who takes ownership, not how the business is valued. Establish the indicative value range first, then discuss deal structure.

materials.name: Business Sale Assessment Framework — The 3-Point Sensitivities
materials.summary: Puts the seller in the purchaser's negotiation seat, so they can see what evidence a buyer needs before they set a price. The underlying method is asset-based, covering tangible assets such as plant and machinery and intangible ones such as goodwill, patents and trademarks — but adding assets and applying a profit multiplier is not enough and leads to overvaluation. Three reality checks test whether the price is bankable for the buyer.
materials.who_when: Owners preparing to sell, and advisors testing whether an asking price a client has in mind will survive a purchaser's scrutiny.
steps: Move the seller into the buyer's seat — the question is not what the business is worth to them, but what evidence a purchaser would need to support that price.
Build the value on an asset base, separating tangible assets (plant, machinery) from intangible ones (goodwill, patents, trademarks).
Refuse the shortcut — adding up assets and applying a profit multiplier on top is insufficient and produces overvaluation.
Apply Serviceability — test the funding calculations to find the finance threshold the business can actually afford to service, including an interest-rate risk assessment.
Apply the Goodwill Repayment Period — how long the purchaser needs to pay back the goodwill component out of the super profits the business generates.
Apply Performance Variance — projected net profits must stay inside a defined variance, so unrealised gains can count, but only within reasonable limits.
Judge the result on one test: is the price bankable for the purchaser? If the three checks say no, the price is not real regardless of what the assets total.

materials.name: Business Valuation — 6-Step Methodology
materials.summary: The working method behind the assessment, from raw financials to an indicative value range. It establishes the true cash available to a buyer, separates super profits from the return the owner should expect anyway, tests the result against the sensitivities, and only then produces a Low / Average / High range built from goodwill, intangibles, tangibles and stock.
materials.who_when: Advisors running an actual valuation for a client — a full sale, a partial sell-down, or a purchase the client is considering.
steps: Gather the core financial and operational data — balance sheet, profit and loss, a full asset list — and a business overview covering competitors, key personnel dependencies, threats and supplier relationships.

Calculate the adjusted net profit by adding back expenses peculiar to the current vendor — depreciation, interest, personal legal fees, owner's wages, sponsorships — to show the free cash flow a purchaser would actually receive.
Choose the earnings basis by buyer type: EBPITDA where the business needs a hands-on owner (the buyer is buying a job), EBITDA for a passive investor looking at distributable free cash flow.
Separate the business into tangible assets, stock and materials, and intangible assets.

Calculate Super Profit — deduct the Minimum Acceptable Cash Surplus from estimated future earnings, where that minimum covers a fair labour rate for the owner, a basic return on invested funds equal to bank interest, a risk premium, and asset replacement reserves.
Check the payback period from Super Profit — under 3 years is Good, 3 to 5 years is Normal, and beyond 5 years warrants caution.

Check serviceability by structuring a hypothetical purchaser loan: take interest, principal, tax and non-cash depreciation off the adjusted earnings and confirm cash still remains to reward the owners.
Check performance variance — to include unrealised gains, the seller must name exactly what performance is yet to be realised, the timeframe, and the specific actions or people needed to deliver it.

Review the other issues and indicators — whether goodwill can genuinely transfer, whether staff agreements carry retention clauses, whether the lease rolls over without hidden reinstatement liabilities, and the extra working capital the buyer will need, such as a 45-day trading reserve.

Establish the indicative value range — apply a risk-adjusted multiplier to adjusted earnings to produce Low, Average and High, with the final assessment combining goodwill, intangible assets, tangible assets, and stock and materials.

advisor_guidance.seller_in_the_buyers_seat: The most powerful reframe in any valuation conversation is to move the seller from defending their asking price to demonstrating it through a buyer's eyes. A seller who cannot answer the buyer's three core questions — can I service this debt, when do I recover my goodwill investment, and is the future growth claim realistic — will lose credibility and the deal.
advisor_guidance.bankable_is_the_test: Revenue and profit alone do not determine whether a business is saleable. The price must be bankable — the cash surplus after all obligations must be sufficient to service the debt a purchaser would take on to buy it. A business with strong revenue but thin margins may produce an asking price no bank will fund.
advisor_guidance.do_not_apply_multipliers_to_goodwill_alo: The single most dangerous valuation error is applying an industry benchmark multiple — drawn from full business sales data — directly to the goodwill component only. This double-counts tangible assets and stock and produces a hyper-inflated figure that will collapse under scrutiny from any informed purchaser or their financier.
advisor_guidance.intangible_asset_transferability_is_ofte: Goodwill value can evaporate quickly if the assets driving it cannot actually be transferred. Social media followings, affiliate programs, platform accounts, and key personnel relationships are frequently counted as intangible value but may be legally or contractually non-transferable. Verify transferability before assigning value.
advisor_guidance.deal_structures_follow_valuation: For MBO, BIMBO, and Newco transactions, the valuation discipline is identical to any other sale. The deal structure determines funding and ownership — not value. Establish the bankable indicative value range first, then work with the appropriate legal and financial advisors to design the deal structure that supports it.
